analysis.one_liner: Lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission set safety standards for firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in February 2019 and stayed there until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently excludes guns and firearm parts from the definition of a "consumer product," which means the Consumer Product Safety Commission — the agency that sets safety rules for toys, cribs, and power tools — is barred from setting safety standards for firearms. This bill strikes that exclusion, allowing the agency to write safety standards for guns and gun components. It was introduced by Rep. Robin Kelly with 23 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who own, handle, or are near firearms would gain a layer of protection the law now withholds: the same agency that recalls defective cribs and car seats could require that guns meet basic safety standards, and defective designs could be recalled. Families affected by accidental shootings and law-enforcement and public-health advocates have long sought this authority.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the legal exclusion that has kept firearms out of the Consumer Product Safety Commission's jurisdiction since the agency was created, permitting it to issue safety standards for guns and firearm components.
Would allow the agency to address hazards in firearm design the way it does for other consumer products, such as manufacturing defects or features shown to cause unintentional discharges.

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers and dealers, who would for the first time face federal product-safety standards, potential recalls, and the compliance costs that come with them. Gun owners could see modest design changes or higher prices if standards required them.

drawbacks.text: Safety standards could raise the cost of firearms, and any new requirement or recall would fall partly on gun owners, including lower-income buyers.

Handing the Consumer Product Safety Commission authority over a product so politically charged could invite aggressive rulemaking that goes well beyond fixing mechanical defects, a concern that has kept guns out of the agency's reach since the 1970s.
Safety standards address defective designs and mechanical hazards, not intentional violence, so the bill would not by itself reduce most firearm deaths.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but incremental: CPSC-style standards mainly prevent accidental deaths and defective designs, a narrow slice of firearm deaths. The costs fall on manufacturers, whose compliance expenses could be passed to buyers. A reasonable design for a product that kills tens of thousands of Americans a year to have no federal safety regulator at all; the strongest honest objection is the risk of political overreach in rulemaking, which the bill's plain language — simply deleting an exclusion — leaves to the agency's judgment.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee from February 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, and the committee never voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Robin Kelly introduced the bill on February 8, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Twenty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a subcommittee or full committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers are better off, because the two-year period in which the bill could have become law passed without committee action, leaving their products the only major consumer product with no federal safety regulator. Supporters of gun-safety regulation gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearm manufacturers, who kept their regulatory exemption

for.name: Robin Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 23 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full committee vote; it received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association and allied gun-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Long opposed giving the Consumer Product Safety Commission any authority over firearms, arguing it could be used to restrict gun availability through regulation rather than legislation.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 supporters — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Guns are the only major consumer product exempt from federal product-safety oversight. The bill would have ended that exemption, exposing manufacturers to safety standards, recalls, and compliance costs their industry has avoided for decades, while ordinary people would gain the same defect-protection the rest of the marketplace has.
